newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Hindus seek purity, peace at hilltop festival.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hindus seek purity, peace at hilltop festival.

text.p: It seemed an unending stream of people of all ages flocking the hills at Sitakunda near Bangladesh's port of Chittagong for an annual religious festival by the country's Hindu minority.

The event, called Sitakunda Mela (fair), was held March 7-9 and combined religious rites and festivities for half a million Hindus from within and outside Bangladesh, according to Hindu preachers and organisers.
"People come from India and Nepal too, but they are not easily identified because they mingle with their Bangladeshi relatives," said Akhil Ranjan Shaha, a 60-year-old devotee.
"I have been coming here for 20 years and every time I felt recharged with new spirit of mind," he told Reuters at the festival.
MORE MYTH THAN HISTORY
There is no dependable history of the Sitakunda Mela, which some people say dates from 500 years ago. How it started has remained a mystery, shrouded by differing opinions.
"It's more of a myth than history," said Sudhamoy Paul, a Hindu teacher. "We have many beliefs but one faith," he added.
He said all Hindus believed that the Sitakunda Mela was a sacred occasion that they must attend once in a lifetime.
The priests say the festival started five centuries ago at a site where a severed arm of Goddess Sati fell from the heavens.
Since then the Hindu believers have set up five Mandirs (temples) at Sitakunda, some 1,500 feet high in the hills, to worship the goddess.
Also on the hills are a Sarobar (sacred fountain) and a smokeless eternal flame. But these two sites are too remote for most visitors.
"I feel a strong urge to come here. It cleans my sins and fills my heart with divine blessings," said businessman Sushil Adhikari.
Nearly 30 percent of the women coming to the Mela are widows, and mostly old. They wear white cotton saris, and some have had their heads shaved.
"It's a great opportunity ... we go back from here with our minds freshened and purified," said 65-year-old Saraju Bala, who came from the faraway district of Barisal on the coast.
But for many it is difficult to perform all the rites because they cannot climb the hills to reach the temples.
"We have to walk up hundreds of steps. I guess I am too old to do that," said Bala, resting herself on a bamboo stick.
AUTHORITIES CARE FOR SECURITY

Local authorities imposed tight security and arranged accommodation for the devotees, but many still slept under the sky. They cooked their own food, bathed in two large ponds and shared common toilets.
"It's an annual event and we make sure there is nothing to disturb the worshippers and others attending the Mela," one police officer said.
"The Mela turns into a confluence of people of all ages, and of all faiths," he added.
Some young boys and girls said they had come to the Mela to have some free time with their sweethearts, their relationships taboo in overwhelmingly Moslem Bangladesh.
"I have come with my boyfriend for a retreat," said an 18-year-old college student. But she shied away quickly.
Only 11 percent of Bangladesh's 120 million people are Hindus, and they enjoy equal religious and social rights but often need to be careful not to hurt Islamic sentiments.
Many Moslems also visit the Mela which lasts up to 10 days, although the main rites are performed in three days.
They come to sell a range of small items from clay dolls to cooking utensils.
"It's a good business. The turnover is sometimes more than expected," said Mohammad Shahidullah of Chittagong.
EXAMPLE OF COMMUNAL HARMONY
The Mela has been a testimony to communal harmony in Bangladesh.
"We never faced any problem. No one intimidated us nor did anyone interfere in our rites," said Paresh Mandol.
He said more Hindus used to come from India in the past but their number dropped following violence at the Babri Mosque.

Moslems in India were outraged by destruction of the 16th century mosque in Ayodhya in India's Uttar Pradesh state in 1992 by hardline Hindus, provoking a wave of violent protest in mainly Moslem Bangladesh.
"Many Hindus (from abroad) still fear there could be a Moslem backlash over the mosque issue," he told Reuters.
Deepak Kanti Chakravarty, a priest, said: "Offering prayers at Chandranath (one of the temples at Sitakunda) helps attain a respectable and peaceful life."
"This is a confluence of people from all faiths. They have been flocking here for centuries and getting blessed."
